questions.explanation: A persistent agent is software permanently installed on the endpoint; a nonpersistent (dissolvable) agent runs temporarily and is removed after the assessment, which suits guests and BYOD.
questions.discriminator_tested: Persistent = permanent; nonpersistent = temporary, suits guests/BYOD.

questions.stem: A security team reviews the log below. What BEST explains why this activity is treated as a high-priority alert even though nothing succeeded?
questions.exhibit:
host: files-archive-02  (decoy; not in DNS, no real users or data)
02:14:07  SMB login       user=administrator  src=10.20.4.31  result=fail
02:14:09  SMB login       user=backup         src=10.20.4.31  result=fail
02:14:15  share listing  requested           src=10.20.4.31

options.text: Nothing legitimate should touch this system
options.rationale: Correct: a decoy has no real use, so any contact is suspicious.

options.text: SMB traffic isn't permitted on internal networks
options.rationale: SMB is normal on internal networks.

options.text: Failed administrator logins can indicate password guessing
options.rationale: True in general, but it doesn't explain why even one touch here is urgent.

options.text: The decoy blocks the attacker and records their tools
options.rationale: A honeypot detects and observes; it isn't a blocking control.

questions.explanation: A honeypot is a decoy system that lures attackers so they can be detected and studied. It has no legitimate use, so any interaction, even a failed one, is suspicious, and 10.20.4.31 is likely compromised.
questions.discriminator_tested: Honeypot has no legitimate use, so any interaction is suspicious.

questions.stem: A user's smartwatch syncs with their phone, and wireless earbuds stream audio from it, all within a couple of meters. Which network type is this?

options.text: WWAN
options.rationale: A WWAN is carrier-scale, across regions.

options.text: WMAN
options.rationale: A WMAN spans a city.

options.text: WLAN
options.rationale: A WLAN covers a building or campus.

options.text: WPAN
options.rationale: Correct: very short range, one person's devices.

questions.explanation: A WPAN (wireless personal area network) has very short range, such as Bluetooth. It is the smallest scale: one person's devices.
questions.discriminator_tested: WPAN = smallest scale, one person's devices.

questions.stem: Which two scenarios describe a WLAN? (Choose two.)

options.text: A home router's Wi-Fi covering the house and yard
options.rationale: Correct: home Wi-Fi is a WLAN.

options.text: A phone pairing with a car's hands-free kit
options.rationale: That is a WPAN.

options.text: A city-wide fixed wireless service linking buildings
options.rationale: That is a WMAN.

options.text: Laptops on Wi-Fi throughout a three-floor office
options.rationale: Correct: Wi-Fi within a building.

options.text: A tablet using a 5G carrier data plan
options.rationale: Carrier cellular coverage is a WWAN.

questions.explanation: A WLAN (wireless local area network) is Wi-Fi within a building or campus, the common enterprise and home wireless scale.
questions.discriminator_tested: WLAN = Wi-Fi within a building or campus.

questions.stem: A city installs point-to-multipoint wireless links that connect its libraries, police stations, and offices across town. Which network type BEST fits?

options.text: WLAN
options.rationale: A WLAN stays within a building or campus.

options.text: WPAN
options.rationale: A WPAN reaches only a few meters.

options.text: WMAN
options.rationale: Correct: city-scale wireless.

options.text: WWAN
options.rationale: A WWAN is carrier-provided across large regions, not a city's own links.

questions.explanation: A WMAN (wireless metropolitan area network) spans a city or large area. It sits between WLAN and WWAN in scale.
questions.discriminator_tested: WMAN is between WLAN and WWAN in scale.

questions.stem: Field technicians need connectivity anywhere in the state, from highways to rural sites, without depending on local Wi-Fi. Which network type should they use?

options.text: A WWAN through a cellular carrier's data service
options.rationale: Correct: carrier coverage over a large region.

options.text: A WMAN covering the company's home city
options.rationale: A WMAN covers a city, not a whole state.

options.text: A WPAN tethered to each technician's laptop
options.rationale: A WPAN only links nearby devices; it provides no wide-area reach itself.

options.text: A WLAN extended with outdoor access points
options.rationale: Outdoor APs still cover only a site.

questions.explanation: A WWAN (wireless wide area network) provides cellular-style coverage over large regions. It is the largest scale and is carrier-provided.
questions.discriminator_tested: WWAN = largest scale; carrier-provided.

questions.stem: A small office already has a wired switch. It buys a device to plug into that switch so laptops in the back room can reach the wired network over Wi-Fi. What is that device?

options.text: A wireless access point
options.rationale: Correct: it bridges wireless clients onto the wired network.

options.text: A Wi-Fi range extender
options.rationale: An extender repeats an existing Wi-Fi signal rather than plugging into the switch.

options.text: A directional antenna
options.rationale: An antenna shapes a signal; it doesn't connect clients by itself.

options.text: A wireless network adapter
options.rationale: That is the client-side hardware in each laptop.

questions.explanation: A wireless access point (WAP) connects wireless clients to the wired network. It is the infrastructure-side bridge; a wireless network access card is the client-side adapter.
questions.discriminator_tested: WAP = infrastructure-side bridge; NIC = client-side.

questions.stem: A laptop can't see any wireless networks, although colleagues nearby can. The technician runs the command below. What is the MOST likely cause?
questions.exhibit:
C:\> netsh wlan show interfaces
    Name            : Wi-Fi
    Description     : Intel(R) Wi-Fi 6 AX201 160MHz
    Physical address: 4c:79:6e:21:aa:10
    State           : disconnected
    Radio status    : Hardware On
                      Software Off

options.text: The access point is not broadcasting its SSID
options.rationale: Colleagues can see networks, and a hidden SSID wouldn't hide all of them.

options.text: The adapter's radio is off in software
options.rationale: Correct: the client-side radio is disabled, so it sees nothing.

options.text: The laptop is not connected to a wireless network
options.rationale: True, but that restates the symptom rather than the cause.

options.text: The adapter doesn't support Wi-Fi 6 networks
options.rationale: The AX201 is a Wi-Fi 6 adapter.

questions.explanation: A wireless network access card is the client-side adapter that lets a device connect wirelessly; the WAP is infrastructure-side. 'Software Off' means the adapter's radio is disabled on the laptop, for example by airplane mode.
questions.discriminator_tested: The wireless NIC is client-side hardware.

questions.stem: A company needs a wireless bridge between two buildings 800 meters apart and wants to keep the signal from spilling across the surrounding neighbourhood. Which antenna choice is BEST?

options.text: The access points' built-in dipole antennas
options.rationale: Built-in dipoles are omnidirectional and low gain.

options.text: A high-gain omnidirectional antenna on each roof
options.rationale: Could reach, but it radiates in all directions, the spill the company wants to avoid.

options.text: More access points spaced between the buildings
options.rationale: Adds coverage everywhere in between, which spreads the signal further.

options.text: A directional antenna at each building
options.rationale: Correct: a focused beam gives long reach with little spill.

questions.explanation: Wireless antennae radiate and receive signal. Omnidirectional antennas cover all directions for wider coverage; directional antennas focus a beam for longer reach and less spill.
questions.discriminator_tested: Directional = focused beam, longer reach.

questions.stem: At a remote site with no access point, two laptops connect directly to each other over Wi-Fi to share files. What is this arrangement?

options.text: An infrastructure BSS
options.rationale: In an infrastructure BSS, traffic goes through an AP.

options.text: An independent BSS (ad hoc)
options.rationale: Correct: peer-to-peer with no AP.

options.text: An extended service set
options.rationale: An ESS links several APs; there are none here.

options.text: A WPAN using Bluetooth
options.rationale: The laptops are using Wi-Fi, not Bluetooth.

questions.explanation: An Independent BSS (ad hoc) has devices connecting directly to each other with no AP: peer-to-peer. In an infrastructure BSS, traffic flows through the AP.
questions.discriminator_tested: IBSS has no AP; peer-to-peer.

questions.stem: A controller shows the status below for the only access point in a small office. What do this AP and its clients form?
questions.exhibit:
AP: AP-Lobby   BSSID: 00:3a:9a:10:22:01   SSID: CorpNet   Channel: 36
Associated clients: 12
Other APs advertising CorpNet: none

options.text: A basic service set
options.rationale: Correct: one AP plus its associated clients.

options.text: An extended service set
options.rationale: An ESS needs two or more APs under one SSID.

options.text: A service set identifier
options.rationale: The SSID is the network's name, not the group of devices.

options.text: An independent BSS
options.rationale: An IBSS has no AP at all.

questions.explanation: A Basic Service Set (BSS) is one AP plus its associated clients, the basic wireless building block, identified by the AP's BSSID. Two or more BSSs sharing an SSID form an ESS.
questions.discriminator_tested: BSS = single AP coverage area.

questions.stem: Two laptops on the same office Wi-Fi exchange files. Each frame travels from the sending laptop to the access point and then from the access point to the receiving laptop. Which arrangement is this?

options.text: Infrastructure BSS
options.rationale: Correct: clients communicate through the AP.

options.text: Bluetooth piconet
options.rationale: The devices are on Wi-Fi.

options.text: Independent BSS
options.rationale: In an IBSS the laptops would talk directly.

options.text: Wi-Fi Direct pairing
options.rationale: Wi-Fi Direct is device to device, without the AP relaying.

questions.explanation: An infrastructure BSS is a BSS in which clients communicate through the AP. In ad hoc (IBSS) mode, clients talk directly with no AP.
questions.discriminator_tested: Infrastructure BSS: traffic flows via the AP.

questions.stem: A manager suggests hiding the office Wi-Fi network's name instead of turning on WPA3, to save effort. What is the BEST response?

options.text: A network name is an identifier, not a security control
options.rationale: Correct: hidden names still show up in probe traffic; encryption and authentication protect the network.

options.text: Hiding it works, since scanners skip hidden networks
options.rationale: Scanners detect hidden networks easily.

options.text: Combine a hidden name with MAC filtering instead
options.rationale: MAC addresses are easily spoofed; neither replaces encryption.

options.text: Hide the name and enable WPA3, since both add strong protection
options.rationale: Enabling WPA3 is right, but hiding the name adds no real protection.

questions.explanation: The Service Set ID (SSID) is the name identifying a wireless network. It is a network name, not a security control: hidden SSIDs still appear in probe traffic, so encryption and authentication do the protecting.
questions.discriminator_tested: SSID is a name, not a security control.

questions.stem: A laptop is carried from the lobby to the warehouse without losing its connection. Based on the scan below, what BEST explains this?
questions.exhibit:
C:\> netsh wlan show networks mode=bssid
SSID 1 : CorpNet
    Authentication : WPA2-Enterprise
    BSSID 1 : 00:3a:9a:10:22:01   Signal 92%   Channel 36
    BSSID 2 : 00:3a:9a:10:41:07   Signal 61%   Channel 149
    BSSID 3 : 00:3a:9a:10:58:0c   Signal 34%   Channel 44

options.text: WPA2-Enterprise lets the laptop keep its session
options.rationale: Authentication type doesn't create coverage across the building.

options.text: The APs form an ad hoc network between themselves
options.rationale: APs in an ESS are linked by a wired distribution system, not ad hoc.

options.text: Several APs share one SSID as an extended service set
options.rationale: Correct: three BSSIDs under one SSID, linked by the wired network, allow roaming.

options.text: The laptop keeps a strong signal from at least one of the APs
options.rationale: True as the walk goes, but it is the shared SSID that makes the handover seamless.

questions.explanation: An Extended Service Set (ESS) is two or more BSSs linked by a wired distribution system under one SSID, which enables roaming. The three BSSIDs advertising CorpNet are one ESS.
questions.discriminator_tested: ESS enables roaming across multiple APs.

questions.stem: A 2.4 GHz survey of one office floor (US) shows the channel plan below. Users near AP-3B and AP-3D report slow, unreliable Wi-Fi. What is the BEST fix?
questions.exhibit:
AP       Band      Channel
AP-3A    2.4 GHz   1
AP-3B    2.4 GHz   4
AP-3C    2.4 GHz   6
AP-3D    2.4 GHz   9
AP-3E    2.4 GHz   11

options.text: Raise the transmit power on AP-3B and AP-3D
options.rationale: More power on overlapping channels makes the interference worse.

options.text: Move clients near those APs onto 5 GHz
options.rationale: Helps those clients, but leaves the overlapping 2.4 GHz plan in place.

options.text: Give AP-3B and AP-3D a different SSID
options.rationale: The network name has no effect on radio overlap.

options.text: Re-plan to use only channels 1, 6, and 11
options.rationale: Correct: 4 and 9 overlap their neighbours; 1, 6, and 11 don't.

questions.explanation: In the 2.4 GHz band there are only three nonoverlapping channels (1, 6, 11 in the US). Channels 4 and 9 overlap their neighbours and cause interference; with so few channels, crowding is common.
questions.discriminator_tested: 2.4 GHz has three nonoverlapping channels: 1, 6, 11.

questions.stem: An older barcode scanner supports only 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi. A new access point is configured for 802.11ac and nothing else. Why can't the scanner connect?

options.text: 802.11ac uses channels 1, 6, and 11 only
options.rationale: Those are 2.4 GHz channels; 802.11ac doesn't use 2.4 GHz.

options.text: 802.11ac needs a directional antenna
options.rationale: Antenna type isn't tied to the standard.

options.text: 802.11ac operates only in the 5 GHz band
options.rationale: Correct: a 2.4 GHz-only device can't see it.

options.text: 802.11ac requires WPA3 support on clients
options.rationale: 802.11ac doesn't mandate a security protocol.

questions.explanation: 802.11ac operates in the 5 GHz band only, with many more nonoverlapping channels and less crowding. A 2.4 GHz-only device can't see it; 802.11n is the standard that spans both bands.
questions.discriminator_tested: 802.11ac is 5 GHz only.

questions.stem: A warehouse has older handhelds that support only 2.4 GHz and newer laptops that work best on 5 GHz. Of the standards listed, which one lets a single AP model serve both groups?

options.rationale: Correct: dual-band, so it serves 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz clients.
5 GHz only, and an older standard.
5 GHz only; the handhelds couldn't connect.
2.4 GHz only; the laptops couldn't use 5 GHz.

questions.explanation: 802.11n operates in either band (dual-band), so it can serve 2.4 GHz-only devices and 5 GHz clients alike. 802.11ac is 5 GHz only.
questions.discriminator_tested: 802.11n spans both bands.

questions.stem: A stadium's Wi-Fi has plenty of bandwidth on paper, but performance collapses when 20,000 fans connect at once. Which upgrade BEST targets this problem?

options.text: More 2.4 GHz APs on channels 1, 6, and 11
options.rationale: Three channels can't carry a stadium crowd.

options.text: WPA3 for a stronger handshake on each client
options.rationale: Security doesn't fix capacity.

options.text: 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6), for efficiency in dense crowds
options.rationale: Correct: built to serve many clients at once efficiently, using OFDMA.

options.text: 802.11ac, for wider channels and higher peak speeds
options.rationale: Raises peak speed, but the problem is serving thousands of clients at once.

questions.explanation: Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) focuses on efficiency in dense environments, using features such as OFDMA to serve many clients at once. Its gains are efficiency and capacity, not just raw speed.
questions.discriminator_tested: Wi-Fi 6 gains are efficiency and capacity, not just raw speed.

questions.stem: Wi-Fi in the break room slows down every day around lunchtime. The AP's statistics are below. What is the MOST likely cause?
questions.exhibit:
AP-Break   Band 2.4 GHz   Channel 6   (mounted beside the staff kitchen)
Time     Retries   Noise floor   Clients
11:50    4%        -92 dBm       9
12:05    41%       -61 dBm       14
12:20    38%       -63 dBm       15
12:40    5%        -91 dBm       8

options.text: Microwave ovens raising noise in the 2.4 GHz band
options.rationale: Correct: the noise floor jumps 30 dB only while the kitchen is busy.

options.text: The AP's WPA2 keys expiring at midday
options.rationale: Key handling doesn't change the noise floor.

options.text: More clients joining the AP at lunchtime
options.rationale: Clients rise modestly; that doesn't explain a 30 dB jump in noise.

options.text: A neighbouring AP overlapping on channel 6
options.rationale: Co-channel overlap would be constant, not just at lunch.

questions.explanation: Interference is signal degradation from other wireless sources or overlapping channels. Non-Wi-Fi sources such as microwave ovens raise the noise floor in 2.4 GHz, which is more exposed than 5 GHz; retries spike only while the noise rises.
questions.discriminator_tested: Non-Wi-Fi sources interfere; 2.4 GHz is more exposed.

questions.stem: A sensor in a detached shed 60 m from the AP, behind two brick walls, needs a reliable but modest-speed connection. Which band BEST fits, and why?

options.text: 5 GHz, because it has more nonoverlapping channels
options.rationale: True of 5 GHz, but channel count doesn't help a weak, obstructed link.

options.text: 2.4 GHz, because it is the faster band
options.rationale: 2.4 GHz is the slower band.

options.text: 5 GHz, because it delivers higher speeds
options.rationale: Higher speed comes with shorter range and worse penetration.

options.text: 2.4 GHz, because it reaches farther through walls
options.rationale: Correct: longer range and better penetration matter more than speed here.

questions.explanation: 2.4 GHz offers longer range and better penetration but is slower; 5 GHz is faster with shorter range. For a distant device behind walls that needs only modest speed, range wins.
questions.discriminator_tested: 2.4 GHz = range; 5 GHz = speed.

questions.stem: A cafe's Wi-Fi is an open network with a captive portal where customers enter a voucher code from their receipt. Which statement BEST describes the protection?

options.text: Users are checked, but traffic is not encrypted
options.rationale: Correct: the portal controls who gets on; the open network leaves traffic unencrypted.

options.text: Traffic is encrypted, but users aren't checked
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: Paying customers are the ones who get access
options.rationale: True, but it says nothing about whether traffic is protected.

options.text: The voucher code encrypts each customer's traffic
options.rationale: A voucher grants access; it isn't an encryption key.

questions.explanation: Authentication verifies who connects; encryption protects the data. They are separate functions: a voucher portal controls who gets on, but on an open network the traffic itself travels unencrypted.
questions.discriminator_tested: Authentication (identity) and encryption (confidentiality) are separate functions.

questions.stem: A wireless audit produces the table below. Which network should be reconfigured FIRST?
questions.exhibit:
SSID          Security          Cipher
Scanners      WEP               WEP-104 (RC4)
Office        WPA2-Personal     CCMP (AES)
Visitors      WPA3-Personal     CCMP (AES)
Engineering   WPA2-Enterprise   CCMP (AES)

options.text: Scanners
options.rationale: Correct: WEP is broken and can be cracked quickly.

options.text: Engineering
options.rationale: WPA2-Enterprise with AES is sound.

options.text: Visitors
options.rationale: Already on the current generation.

options.text: Office
options.rationale: Could move to WPA3 later, but WPA2 with AES isn't broken.

questions.explanation: WEP, the original wireless security, uses RC4 with a short initialization vector. It is broken and obsolete and never acceptable, so it is replaced first; WPA2 networks can move to WPA3 later.
questions.discriminator_tested: WEP is broken and obsolete; never acceptable.

questions.stem: An audit finds a legacy access point still configured for WPA with TKIP. What is the BEST reason to upgrade it?

options.text: WPA uses a short IV that cracks within minutes
options.rationale: That describes WEP.

options.text: WPA sends traffic without encryption
options.rationale: WPA does encrypt, using TKIP.

options.text: WPA was a stopgap for old hardware, replaced by WPA2
options.rationale: Correct: an interim fix, superseded by WPA2 with AES.

options.text: TKIP is slower than modern ciphers on busy networks
options.rationale: Performance suffers too, but the security weakness is the real reason.

questions.explanation: WPA was the interim replacement for WEP, using TKIP so it could run on legacy hardware. It was a stopgap, superseded by WPA2 with AES.
questions.discriminator_tested: WPA/TKIP was a stopgap superseded by WPA2.

questions.stem: An access point is configured with the settings below. Which security configuration is it using?
questions.exhibit:
ssid=Office
wpa=2
wpa_key_mgmt=WPA-PSK
rsn_pairwise=CCMP
wpa_passphrase=Spring2026!

options.text: WPA2-Enterprise with per-user RADIUS logins
options.rationale: Enterprise would use 802.1X (WPA-EAP), not a passphrase.

options.text: WPA with TKIP and a shared passphrase
options.rationale: The cipher is CCMP, not TKIP.

options.text: WPA2-Personal with AES-CCMP
options.rationale: Correct: WPA-PSK key management with CCMP (AES) and a shared passphrase.

options.text: WPA3-Personal using SAE with a passphrase
options.rationale: WPA3-Personal would show SAE key management.

questions.explanation: WPA2 uses AES-CCMP and is the long-standing standard; Personal mode uses one shared passphrase (WPA-PSK). Enterprise would use 802.1X, and WPA3-Personal would use SAE.
questions.discriminator_tested: WPA2-Personal = AES-CCMP with a shared passphrase.

questions.stem: A company of 400 staff shares one Wi-Fi passphrase. Each time someone leaves, IT has to change it on every device. Which change BEST solves this?

options.text: Change the passphrase monthly instead
options.rationale: Still a shared key; a leaver keeps access until the next change.

options.text: WPA2-Enterprise with 802.1X and RADIUS accounts
options.rationale: Correct: each user has their own credentials, so a leaver's account is simply disabled.

options.text: Hide the SSID so former staff won't find it
options.rationale: Hidden SSIDs are easily found, and the leaver still knows the key.

options.text: WPA3-Personal with a longer shared passphrase
options.rationale: Stronger, but still one shared key to change when someone leaves.

questions.explanation: WPA2-Enterprise uses 802.1X authentication against a RADIUS server, so each user has individual credentials rather than one shared key; disabling a leaver's account removes only their access.
questions.discriminator_tested: WPA2-Enterprise = individual credentials per user.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST describes how 802.11i relates to WPA2?

options.text: 802.11i is a faster Wi-Fi standard than WPA2
options.rationale: 802.11i is about security, not speed.

options.text: Both describe AES-based Wi-Fi security
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't state how they relate.

options.text: 802.11i is the IEEE standard; WPA2 certifies it
options.rationale: Correct: WPA2 is the Wi-Fi Alliance certification of 802.11i.

options.text: WPA2 is the IEEE standard; 802.11i certifies it
options.rationale: This is reversed.

questions.explanation: 802.11i is the IEEE standard for wireless security that WPA2 implements. WPA2 is the Wi-Fi Alliance certification of it.
questions.discriminator_tested: 802.11i is the standard; WPA2 is its certification.

questions.stem: Which two are improvements WPA3 brings over WPA2? (Choose two.)

options.text: A stronger handshake that replaces PSK
options.rationale: Correct: SAE replaces the PSK handshake.

options.text: Support for both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands
options.rationale: Band support comes from the radio standard, such as 802.11n.

options.text: Hiding the SSID from scanners
options.rationale: SSID hiding isn't a WPA3 feature or a security control.

options.text: AES encryption of wireless traffic
options.rationale: WPA2 already uses AES.

options.text: Resistance to offline password guessing
options.rationale: Correct: a captured handshake no longer allows offline cracking.

questions.explanation: WPA3 is the current generation, with a stronger handshake and protections than WPA2. It replaces the PSK handshake and resists offline password guessing; AES was already part of WPA2.
questions.discriminator_tested: WPA3 replaces the PSK handshake and resists offline guessing.

questions.stem: An access point is configured with the settings below. Which security mode does it set up?
questions.exhibit:
ssid=Studio
wpa=2
wpa_key_mgmt=SAE
ieee80211w=2
rsn_pairwise=CCMP
sae_password=Lantern-Orbit-42

options.text: WPA2-Personal using PSK
options.rationale: WPA2-Personal would show WPA-PSK, not SAE.

options.text: WPA3-Personal using SAE
options.rationale: Correct: SAE key management with a passphrase, plus required management-frame protection.

options.text: WPA3-Enterprise using 802.1X
options.rationale: Enterprise would use 802.1X and a RADIUS server, not a password.

options.text: WEP using a long static key
options.rationale: WEP doesn't use SAE or CCMP.

questions.explanation: WPA3-Personal is passphrase-based WPA3 using SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) instead of WPA2's PSK handshake. key_mgmt=SAE gives it away; WPA3 also requires protected management frames (ieee80211w=2).
questions.discriminator_tested: WPA3-Personal uses SAE instead of PSK.

questions.stem: A defense contractor must protect its Wi-Fi to the highest available standard and authenticate each user individually. Which mode BEST fits?

options.text: WPA3-Enterprise in 192-bit mode
options.rationale: Correct: per-user 802.1X plus the high-security cryptographic suite.

options.text: WPA2-Enterprise with RADIUS
options.rationale: Per-user, but the previous generation.

options.text: WPA3-Enterprise with default settings
options.rationale: Strong and per-user, but not the highest available level.

options.text: WPA3-Personal with a long passphrase
options.rationale: A shared passphrase doesn't authenticate users individually.

questions.explanation: WPA3-Enterprise uses 802.1X/RADIUS for per-user authentication with stronger cryptography. Its optional 192-bit mode is intended for high-security environments.
questions.discriminator_tested: WPA3-Enterprise 192-bit mode is for high-security use.

questions.stem: An admin needs to stop the internet from reaching the HR database while still letting web traffic reach the public web server. Which device's core job is this?

options.text: A proxy server
options.rationale: A proxy makes requests on clients' behalf; it isn't the boundary policy device.

options.text: A firewall
options.rationale: Correct: it permits or denies traffic between networks by rule.

options.text: A wireless access point
options.rationale: An AP connects wireless clients; it doesn't filter traffic between networks.

options.text: An IDS
options.rationale: An IDS alerts on suspicious traffic; it doesn't enforce rules.

questions.explanation: A firewall permits or denies traffic between networks based on rules: boundary enforcement by policy. An IDS only alerts, and a proxy acts for clients at the application level.
questions.discriminator_tested: Firewall = boundary enforcement by policy.

questions.stem: After this ACL was applied inbound on a router's internet-facing interface, staff inside can no longer load external websites. The router keeps no connection table. What is the MOST likely reason?
questions.exhibit:
access-list 110 permit tcp any host 203.0.113.20 eq 443
access-list 110 deny   ip any any
!
interface Gi0/0
 description Internet
 ip access-group 110 in

options.text: The deny rule drops whatever isn't explicitly allowed
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say which traffic is being dropped or why it matters.

options.text: Port 443 can be used by one host at a time
options.rationale: Many hosts use port 443 simultaneously.

options.text: Replies to staff requests match no permit rule
options.rationale: Correct: without session memory, return traffic needs its own permit rule.

options.text: The ACL blocks staff's outbound HTTPS requests
options.rationale: It is applied inbound; outbound requests leave fine.

questions.explanation: A stateless (packet-filtering) firewall judges each packet alone on IP, port, and protocol. It has no memory of sessions, so return traffic needs its own permit rule; a stateful firewall would allow the replies automatically.
questions.discriminator_tested: Stateless: no memory of sessions; every packet needs a matching rule.

questions.stem: What BEST explains why a stateful firewall needs fewer rules than a stateless one to let internal users browse the web?

options.text: It tracks sessions and admits their return traffic
options.rationale: Correct: replies to established sessions are allowed automatically.

options.text: It drops inbound traffic unless it is web traffic
options.rationale: That would be a rule, not a reason fewer rules are needed.

options.text: It inspects packets more thoroughly than a stateless filter
options.rationale: Vaguely true, but session tracking is the specific reason.

options.text: It identifies applications rather than ports
options.rationale: That describes a next-generation firewall.

questions.explanation: A stateful firewall tracks connection state and allows return traffic for established sessions. A stateless firewall remembers nothing, so each direction needs its own rule.
questions.discriminator_tested: Stateful remembers sessions; contrast with stateless.

questions.stem: All three sessions in the log below use TCP 443, yet the device treats them differently. What type of device produced this log?
questions.exhibit:
rule    src          dst              port  app-id                action
r-web   10.1.5.22    198.51.100.10    443   web-browsing          allow
r-web   10.1.5.22    198.51.100.20    443   bittorrent            deny
r-web   10.1.5.31    192.0.2.50       443   cloud-storage-upload  deny

options.text: A stateless packet filter
options.rationale: A packet filter sees only addresses and ports.

options.text: A next-generation firewall
options.rationale: Correct: it identifies the application, not just the port.

options.text: An intrusion detection system
options.rationale: An IDS alerts; it doesn't allow or deny sessions.

options.text: A stateful firewall
options.rationale: A stateful firewall sees ports and sessions, so all three would look alike.

questions.explanation: A next-generation firewall (NGFW) adds application awareness, deep packet inspection, and integrated IPS. It sees applications, not just ports, which is how it tells web browsing from BitTorrent on the same port.
questions.discriminator_tested: NGFW sees applications, not just ports.

questions.stem: A salesperson's laptop is used on hotel and airport Wi-Fi. Which firewall BEST protects it there?

options.text: The hotel's network firewall, which isolates guests
options.rationale: The company doesn't control it, and guests share the network.

options.text: A host-based firewall, because it travels with the laptop
options.rationale: Correct: it protects the device wherever it is.

options.text: A host-based firewall, because it filters more ports
options.rationale: Right device, wrong reason: it isn't about port count.

options.text: A network firewall, once the VPN connects to the office
options.rationale: Covers traffic in the tunnel, but not the laptop on the hotel network before or outside it.

questions.explanation: A host-based firewall runs on one endpoint and protects that device wherever it is; a network-based firewall sits at a network boundary and protects a whole segment.
questions.discriminator_tested: Host-based protects one device; network-based protects a segment.

questions.stem: A hospital wants alerts about suspicious traffic on its clinical network but won't accept any device that could drop or delay traffic to patient monitors. Which option BEST fits?

options.text: A stateless firewall with logging
options.rationale: A firewall sits in the path and filters traffic.

options.text: An IDS fed by a SPAN port copy
options.rationale: Correct: it watches a copy, so it can never block or delay the real traffic.

options.text: An IPS set to alert without blocking
options.rationale: Can alert without blocking, but an inline device can still fail and disrupt traffic.

options.text: An inline IPS that blocks attacks
options.rationale: Blocking in the path is exactly what the hospital refuses.

questions.explanation: An IDS monitors traffic, typically a passive copy, and alerts on suspicious activity; it detects and alerts only. An IPS sits inline, so a failure can disrupt traffic.
questions.discriminator_tested: IDS detects and alerts only; does not block.

questions.stem: Users report a 38-second network outage at 10:52. Given the sensor log below, what BEST explains it?
questions.exhibit:
10:41:12 sig 41022 "SMB remote code execution attempt" src 10.8.3.14 dst 10.8.1.5:445 action=DROP
10:41:12 sensor eth1-eth2 inline  mode=prevention  fail-mode=closed
10:52:40 sensor process restart
10:52:40 traffic on eth1-eth2 halted for 00:00:38

options.text: A passive IDS lost its copy of the traffic
options.rationale: Losing a passive copy can't interrupt users' traffic.

options.text: A device in the traffic path briefly stopped forwarding
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't say why: the inline sensor's fail-closed restart.

options.text: The SMB exploit crashed the file server
options.rationale: That attempt was dropped at 10:41, eleven minutes earlier.

options.text: The inline sensor restarted while set to fail closed
options.rationale: Correct: an inline device that fails closed stops traffic while it recovers.

questions.explanation: An IPS sits inline and blocks detected malicious traffic. Because it sits in the path, a sensor failure can disrupt traffic; with fail-mode closed, traffic stops until the sensor recovers.
questions.discriminator_tested: IPS is inline; a failure can disrupt traffic.

questions.stem: A brand-new attack with no published signature slips past one sensor but is flagged by another, because a server suddenly sent 40 times its usual outbound volume at 3 a.m. Which detection method caught it?

options.text: Stateful inspection
options.rationale: Stateful inspection tracks sessions; it doesn't judge volume against a baseline.

options.text: Anomaly-based detection
options.rationale: Correct: it flagged a deviation from the server's baseline.

options.text: Honeypot monitoring
options.rationale: The server is a production system, not a decoy.

options.text: Signature-based detection
options.rationale: There was no signature to match; that's why the first sensor missed it.

questions.explanation: Signature-based detection matches known patterns, so it misses novel attacks. Anomaly-based detection flags deviation from a baseline and catches them, at the cost of more false positives.
questions.discriminator_tested: Signature misses novel attacks; anomaly catches them with more false positives.

questions.stem: A security analyst reviews the log below. What type of device produced it?
questions.exhibit:
10:02:11 user=amartin  GET https://news.example.com/      category=News        action=ALLOW
10:02:47 user=amartin  GET https://casino.example.net/    category=Gambling    action=BLOCK
10:03:05 user=tlee     GET https://drive.example.org/up   category=File-share  action=BLOCK

options.text: An IDS alerting on users' suspicious requests
options.rationale: An IDS doesn't block requests.

options.text: A DNS resolver blocking names on a blocklist
options.rationale: DNS sees hostnames only, not the user or the full URL path.

options.text: A web proxy filtering requests for users
options.rationale: Correct: it sees users, full URLs, and categories because it makes the requests on their behalf.

options.text: A stateless firewall filtering on IP and port
options.rationale: A packet filter can't see users, full URLs, or content categories.

questions.explanation: A proxy server or web filter is an intermediary that makes requests for clients and can filter content. It works at the application level, so it sees full URLs, users, and categories, which a packet filter can't.
questions.discriminator_tested: Proxy works at the application level on behalf of clients.

questions.stem: An incident register lists the entries below. Which two are primarily violations of integrity? (Choose two.)
questions.exhibit:
INC-101  Web server unreachable for 3 hours after a power failure
INC-102  Payroll file's bank details altered by an unknown process
INC-103  Laptop holding an unencrypted customer list stolen from a car
INC-104  Database rows silently changed by a faulty sync script
INC-105  Executives' email read by an intercepting proxy

options.text: INC-104
options.rationale: Correct: unauthorized change, even though it was accidental.

options.text: INC-105
options.rationale: Reading someone's email is eavesdropping: confidentiality.

options.text: INC-101
options.rationale: An outage is an availability problem.

options.text: INC-103
options.rationale: Exposure of data is a confidentiality problem.

options.text: INC-102
options.rationale: Correct: data was changed without authorization.

questions.explanation: The CIA triad is confidentiality (no unauthorized disclosure), integrity (no unauthorized change), and availability (accessible when needed). Altered payroll details and silently changed rows are integrity violations, whatever the intent.
questions.discriminator_tested: Tampering = integrity, even when accidental.

questions.stem: Which two controls MOST directly reduce the risk from people who already have legitimate access to company systems? (Choose two.)

options.text: Least-privilege access for each role
options.rationale: Correct: limits what any one insider can reach.

options.text: Logging and review of user activity
options.rationale: Correct: makes misuse visible and deters it.

options.text: Hiding the corporate SSID
options.rationale: Insiders already know it, and hiding isn't a security control.

options.text: Intrusion prevention at the internet edge
options.rationale: Guards the edge; insider activity never crosses it.

options.text: A stronger perimeter firewall
options.rationale: Insiders are already past the perimeter.

questions.explanation: Internal threats originate from people or systems inside the organization. They already have legitimate access and may be malicious or accidental, so perimeter controls don't touch them; limiting and watching that access does.
questions.discriminator_tested: Internal threats already have legitimate access.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes an external threat from an internal one?

options.text: It causes more damage than internal threats do
options.rationale: Insiders often cause the most damage.

options.text: It originates from people who are not employees
options.rationale: Close, but contractors with granted access count as internal.

options.text: It must first get past the perimeter
options.rationale: Correct: it starts with no legitimate access.

options.text: It is carried out by criminals rather than by staff members
options.rationale: Insiders can be criminals too; the source is what matters.

questions.explanation: External threats originate outside the organization and must first get past the perimeter; internal threats already have legitimate access.
questions.discriminator_tested: External threats must first get past the perimeter.

questions.stem: A switch logs the sequence below when a device is plugged into port Gi1/0/14. What BEST describes how the network handled the device?
questions.exhibit:
Gi1/0/14  EAPOL start        MAC 3c:52:82:aa:10:7e
Gi1/0/14  auth dot1x         result=FAIL (no supplicant response)
Gi1/0/14  fallback MAB       MAC 3c:52:82:aa:10:7e  result=SUCCESS (known printer)
Gi1/0/14  policy applied     VLAN 40 (printers), ACL PRINT-ONLY

options.text: It identified the device before letting it on the network
options.rationale: True, but it leaves out the policy-based placement that followed.

options.text: It rejected the printer because the 802.1X login failed
options.rationale: The fallback succeeded and the printer was admitted.

options.text: It admitted a known printer to a restricted segment by policy
options.rationale: Correct: identity was established by fallback, and policy decided where it goes.

options.text: It checked the printer's patch level and antivirus status
options.rationale: No health checks appear in the log.

questions.explanation: Network Access Control (NAC) decides whether a device or user may join the network based on identity and policy. When 802.1X failed, the switch fell back to MAC authentication, recognized the printer, and applied the printer policy.
questions.discriminator_tested: NAC enforces policy at connection time.

questions.stem: A NAC policy refuses network access to laptops whose antivirus definitions are more than three days old. Which risk does this check MOST directly reduce?

options.text: Attackers intercepting traffic on the wireless network
options.rationale: Encryption addresses interception.

options.text: Unauthorized users signing in to the network
options.rationale: Who signs in is an identity check, not a health check.

options.text: Unhealthy devices bringing malware onto the network
options.rationale: Correct: it keeps non-compliant endpoints off until they are fixed.

options.text: Users visiting gambling sites during work hours
options.rationale: A web filter handles that.

questions.explanation: Posture assessment checks a device's health and compliance (patches, antivirus, configuration) before or during access. Non-compliant devices are denied, quarantined, or remediated.
questions.discriminator_tested: Posture assessment checks device health, not identity.

questions.stem: The firewall rules for the guest VLAN are below, evaluated top to bottom. Which rule MOST clearly defeats the purpose of a guest network?
questions.exhibit:
Guest VLAN 50 rules
1  permit  VLAN50 -> 10.0.0.53     udp/tcp 53   (internal DNS resolver)
2  permit  VLAN50 -> 10.0.0.0/8    any
3  permit  VLAN50 -> internet      tcp 80, 443
4  deny    VLAN50 -> any           any

options.text: Rule 4
options.rationale: The final deny is good practice.

options.text: Rule 1
options.rationale: A small exposure that could use an external resolver instead, but it allows only DNS to one host.

options.text: Rule 3
options.rationale: Internet web access is what a guest network is for.

options.text: Rule 2
options.rationale: Correct: it opens the entire internal network to guests.

questions.explanation: A guest network is a separate, restricted segment for visitors, isolated from internal resources; internet-only access is typical. Rule 2 lets guests reach the whole internal 10.0.0.0/8 network.
questions.discriminator_tested: Guest network is isolated from internal resources.

questions.stem: Which two statements describe persistent NAC agents? (Choose two.)

options.text: They suit guests and personally owned devices
options.rationale: That is where nonpersistent agents fit.

options.text: They suit IT-managed company devices
options.rationale: Correct: the organization controls what is installed.

options.text: They replace the need for a NAC server
options.rationale: Agents report to a NAC server; they don't replace it.

options.text: They remove themselves after each assessment
options.rationale: That describes a nonpersistent agent.

options.text: They stay installed on the endpoint between sessions
options.rationale: Correct: permanent software on the device.

questions.explanation: A persistent agent is software permanently installed on the endpoint; a nonpersistent agent is temporary and removed after the assessment, which suits guests and BYOD.
questions.discriminator_tested: Persistent = permanent; nonpersistent = temporary.

questions.stem: Which setup BEST lets a security team detect an attacker who is already moving between systems inside the network?

options.text: An IDS sensor on the core switch's SPAN port
options.rationale: Useful detection, but it is not a decoy and must separate real from bad traffic.

options.text: A decoy server on the internet, logging scans for research
options.rationale: Studies outside attackers, but won't see movement inside the network.

options.text: A production file server with extra logging
options.rationale: Real users generate constant legitimate noise there.

options.text: A decoy server on an internal segment, with alerts on any contact
options.rationale: Correct: nothing legitimate touches it, so any internal contact is a strong signal.

questions.explanation: A honeypot is a decoy system that lures attackers so they can be detected and studied. It has no legitimate use, so any interaction is suspicious, which makes an internal honeypot a sharp detector of lateral movement.
questions.discriminator_tested: Honeypot: no legitimate use, so any interaction is suspicious.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST separates a WPAN from a WLAN?

options.text: A WPAN serves one person's devices nearby
options.rationale: Correct: scale is the defining difference.

options.text: A WPAN typically uses Bluetooth rather than Wi-Fi
options.rationale: Common, but the defining feature is scale, not the technology.

options.text: A WPAN needs an access point to connect devices
options.rationale: WPAN devices usually pair directly.

options.text: A WPAN covers a city; a WLAN covers a building
options.rationale: City scale describes a WMAN.

questions.explanation: A WPAN (wireless personal area network) has very short range, such as Bluetooth. It is the smallest scale: one person's devices; a WLAN covers a building or campus.
questions.discriminator_tested: WPAN = smallest scale: one person's devices.

questions.stem: A small business wants staff laptops, phones, and handheld scanners to connect anywhere in its single-floor office and loading dock, using equipment it owns. Which network type BEST fits?

options.text: A WLAN built with the company's own access points
options.rationale: Correct: building-scale Wi-Fi the company controls.

options.text: A WMAN, connecting the office to nearby buildings
options.rationale: There is only one site to cover.

options.text: A WWAN, giving each device its own carrier data plan
options.rationale: Would work, but it is carrier-provided, costs per device, and isn't company-owned.

options.text: A WPAN, pairing each device with one central hub
options.rationale: A WPAN's few meters can't cover an office and dock.

questions.explanation: A WLAN (wireless local area network) is Wi-Fi within a building or campus, the common enterprise and home wireless scale.
questions.discriminator_tested: WLAN is the common enterprise/home wireless scale.

questions.stem: Which of these is BEST described as a WMAN?

options.text: A city's wireless links joining offices across town
options.rationale: Correct: city scale.

options.text: A Bluetooth link from a phone to a headset
options.rationale: That is a WPAN.

options.text: A Wi-Fi network covering a university campus
options.rationale: Campus Wi-Fi is a WLAN.

options.text: A carrier's 5G service across several states
options.rationale: Carrier coverage across regions is a WWAN.

questions.explanation: A WMAN (wireless metropolitan area network) spans a city or large area. It sits between WLAN and WWAN in scale.
questions.discriminator_tested: WMAN spans a city.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes a WWAN from a WMAN?

options.text: A WWAN is built from the company's own Wi-Fi APs
options.rationale: That describes a WLAN.

options.text: A WWAN is carrier-provided, region-wide
options.rationale: Correct: the largest scale, from a carrier.

options.text: A WWAN covers a single city and its suburbs
options.rationale: City scale is a WMAN.

options.text: A WWAN usually costs more per device to run
options.rationale: Often true, but cost isn't what defines it.

questions.explanation: A WWAN (wireless wide area network) provides cellular-style coverage over large regions; it is the largest scale and carrier-provided. A WMAN spans a city.
questions.discriminator_tested: WWAN = largest scale; carrier-provided.

questions.stem: Laptops join the office Wi-Fi with full signal but can't reach any wired servers or the internet. The access point's uplink port shows no link light. Which function is failing?

options.text: The AP's bridge to the wired network
options.rationale: Correct: clients associate, but the AP can't pass their traffic onward.

options.text: The SSID broadcast settings on the AP
options.rationale: Clients found and joined the network.

options.text: The laptops' wireless network adapters
options.rationale: They connected with full signal, so the client side works.

options.text: The access point's radio and antennas
options.rationale: Full signal shows the radio side is fine.

questions.explanation: A wireless access point connects wireless clients to the wired network; it is the bridge between wireless and wired. With its uplink down, clients can associate but their traffic goes nowhere.
questions.discriminator_tested: WAP bridges wireless and wired.

questions.stem: A desktop PC in a room with good Wi-Fi coverage has only an Ethernet port, and no cable can be run to it. What does the PC need in order to join the network?

options.text: A directional antenna
options.rationale: An antenna is no use without a wireless adapter to attach it to.

options.text: A wireless network adapter
options.rationale: Correct: the client-side hardware the PC lacks.

options.text: A wireless access point
options.rationale: The room already has coverage; the AP is the infrastructure side.

options.text: A new SSID for the network
options.rationale: A name change doesn't give the PC a radio.

questions.explanation: A wireless network access card is the client-side adapter that lets a device connect wirelessly. The WAP is the infrastructure-side device.
questions.discriminator_tested: Wireless NIC = client-side hardware.

questions.stem: Which statement BEST compares omnidirectional and directional antennas?

options.text: Omni antennas reach farther than directional ones
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: Directional antennas are for 5 GHz use
options.rationale: Both types exist for both bands.

options.text: Directional antennas give a stronger signal
options.rationale: True within their beam, but weaker everywhere else.

options.text: Omni spreads coverage around; directional reaches farther
options.rationale: Correct: wide coverage versus a focused, longer beam.

questions.explanation: Wireless antennae radiate and receive signal. Omnidirectional antennas cover all directions for wider coverage; directional antennas focus a beam for longer reach.
questions.discriminator_tested: Omni = all directions; directional = focused beam, longer reach.

questions.stem: At a disaster site with no access point, rescuers' laptops share maps over Wi-Fi with each other. One laptop also shares its cellular connection with a phone over Bluetooth. How are the laptops' Wi-Fi links arranged?

options.text: As a WPAN, because Bluetooth is involved
options.rationale: The Bluetooth link is separate; the laptops share maps over Wi-Fi.

options.text: As an extended service set across the site
options.rationale: An ESS links multiple APs; there are none.

options.text: As an infrastructure BSS around one laptop
options.rationale: An infrastructure BSS needs an access point.

options.text: As an independent BSS, peer to peer
options.rationale: Correct: Wi-Fi with no AP is ad hoc.

questions.explanation: An Independent BSS (ad hoc) has devices connecting directly to each other with no AP: peer-to-peer. The Bluetooth tether is a separate WPAN link.
questions.discriminator_tested: IBSS: no AP; peer-to-peer.

questions.stem: Three access points all broadcast the same network name. Which identifier distinguishes each AP's basic service set from the others?

options.text: The SSID, the network's name
options.rationale: All three share the same SSID.

options.text: The BSSID, the AP radio's MAC address
options.rationale: Correct: each BSS has its own BSSID.

options.text: The channel each AP uses
options.rationale: Channels can repeat across APs; they don't identify a BSS.

options.text: The clients' IP addresses
options.rationale: Client addressing has nothing to do with the BSS identity.

questions.explanation: A Basic Service Set (BSS) is one AP plus its associated clients, the basic wireless building block, identified by its BSSID (the AP radio's MAC address). The SSID is shared by every BSS in an ESS.
questions.discriminator_tested: A BSS is a single AP's coverage, identified by its BSSID.

questions.stem: In an infrastructure BSS, laptop A sends a file to laptop B on the same Wi-Fi network. Which path do the frames take?

options.text: Laptop A to the AP, then the AP to laptop B
options.rationale: Correct: clients communicate through the AP.

options.text: Laptop A to the switch, then to laptop B
options.rationale: Wireless clients reach the network through the AP first.

options.text: Laptop A to the internet router and back
options.rationale: Local traffic doesn't need to leave via the router.

options.text: Laptop A directly to laptop B over the air
options.rationale: Direct links are ad hoc (IBSS).

questions.explanation: An infrastructure BSS is a BSS in which clients communicate through the AP; in ad hoc mode, they talk directly with no AP.
questions.discriminator_tested: Infrastructure BSS: traffic flows via the AP.

questions.stem: IT says the second network below is 'secured because it is hidden'. Based on this scan, which statement is BEST?
questions.exhibit:
SSID 1 : CorpNet    Auth WPA2-Enterprise   BSSID 00:3a:9a:10:22:01
SSID 2 :            Auth WPA2-Personal     BSSID 00:3a:9a:10:22:05
SSID 3 : Guest      Auth Open              BSSID 00:3a:9a:10:22:09

options.text: It uses WPA2-Personal, which is weaker than Enterprise
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't address the claim that hiding secures it.

options.text: It is invisible to scanners, so attackers won't find it
options.rationale: The scan shows it plainly.

options.text: Hiding the name doesn't hide the network
options.rationale: Correct: it still beacons and appears in the scan; only the name is blank.

options.text: It belongs to the CorpNet ESS because the BSSIDs match
options.rationale: The BSSIDs differ, and an ESS shares one SSID.

questions.explanation: The SSID is the name identifying a wireless network; it is a network name, not a security control. A hidden network still beacons with its BSSID and shows up in scans with a blank name.
questions.discriminator_tested: SSID is a name, not a security control.

questions.stem: Users lose their connection each time they walk between the two wings of a building. The east wing's AP broadcasts 'Wing-A' and the west wing's AP broadcasts 'Wing-B'. Which change BEST lets them roam?

options.text: Hide both SSIDs so laptops choose the strongest AP by themselves
options.rationale: Hiding names doesn't merge two networks into one.

options.text: Give both APs the same SSID and security settings
options.rationale: Correct: one SSID across linked APs forms an ESS.

options.text: Raise both APs' power so their coverage overlaps
options.rationale: Overlap helps, but clients still won't move between two different networks.

options.text: Set up the laptops as an ad hoc network
options.rationale: Ad hoc removes the APs and the wired network altogether.

questions.explanation: An Extended Service Set (ESS) is two or more BSSs linked by a wired distribution system under one SSID. That shared SSID is what enables roaming across multiple APs.
questions.discriminator_tested: ESS = multiple BSSs under one SSID; enables roaming.

questions.stem: What is the BEST explanation for why channel crowding is more common in 2.4 GHz than in 5 GHz?

options.text: It uses wider channels than 5 GHz does
options.rationale: 5 GHz supports the wider channels.

options.text: It has only three nonoverlapping channels
options.rationale: Correct: 1, 6, and 11 in the US, so neighbours collide.

options.text: It is the band WPA3 requires
options.rationale: WPA3 works in both bands.

options.text: More household devices also use 2.4 GHz
options.rationale: True, but that is non-Wi-Fi interference rather than channel crowding.

questions.explanation: In the 2.4 GHz band there are only three nonoverlapping channels (1, 6, 11 in the US). With so few channels, crowding is common; 5 GHz has many more.
questions.discriminator_tested: Few channels, so crowding is common.

questions.stem: Which two statements about 802.11ac are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: It works in both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz
options.rationale: That describes 802.11n.

options.text: It has many more nonoverlapping channels than 2.4 GHz
options.rationale: Correct: less crowding than 2.4 GHz.

options.text: It operates in the 5 GHz band
options.rationale: Correct: 802.11ac is 5 GHz only.

options.text: It uses channels 1, 6, and 11
options.rationale: Those are 2.4 GHz channels.

options.text: It is also known as Wi-Fi 6
options.rationale: Wi-Fi 6 is 802.11ax.

questions.explanation: 802.11ac operates in 5 GHz only, with many more nonoverlapping channels and less crowding. 802.11n is the dual-band standard, and Wi-Fi 6 is 802.11ax.
questions.discriminator_tested: 802.11ac is 5 GHz only, with more channels.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes 802.11n from 802.11ac?

options.text: 802.11n works in both bands; 802.11ac uses 5 GHz alone
options.rationale: Correct: 802.11n is the dual-band standard.

options.text: 802.11ac is the newer, faster standard
options.rationale: True, but speed and age aren't the band difference the question is after.

options.text: 802.11n uses 5 GHz alone; 802.11ac uses both bands
options.rationale: This is reversed.

options.text: 802.11n is the same as Wi-Fi 6
options.rationale: Wi-Fi 6 is 802.11ax.

questions.explanation: 802.11n operates in either band (dual-band); 802.11ac operates in 5 GHz only. 802.11n is the standard that spans both bands.
questions.discriminator_tested: 802.11n spans both bands; 802.11ac is 5 GHz only.

questions.stem: Which two features BEST describe what Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) improves? (Choose two.)

options.text: Moving to the 5 GHz band alone
options.rationale: That describes 802.11ac.

options.text: OFDMA to serve several clients at once
options.rationale: Correct: one transmission can carry data for several clients.

options.text: Efficiency when many clients share an AP
options.rationale: Correct: built for dense environments.

options.text: Higher peak speed for one client on its own
options.rationale: Peak speed did rise, but the focus is efficiency and capacity.

options.text: Hiding the SSID by default
options.rationale: Not a Wi-Fi 6 feature, and not a security control.

questions.explanation: Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) focuses on efficiency in dense environments, using features such as OFDMA. Its gains are efficiency and capacity, not just raw speed.
questions.discriminator_tested: Wi-Fi 6 gains are efficiency and capacity, not just raw speed.

questions.stem: A warehouse's 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi suffers whenever nearby cordless phones and microwave equipment are in use. Which change BEST reduces the interference?

options.text: Rename the SSID to avoid the conflict
options.rationale: The name has no effect on interference.

options.text: Change the AP to a different 2.4 GHz channel
options.rationale: May help a little, but these sources affect much of the 2.4 GHz band.

options.text: Switch from WPA2 to WPA3 on the network
options.rationale: Security settings don't affect radio interference.

options.text: Move capable clients and APs to the 5 GHz band
options.rationale: Correct: those sources sit in 2.4 GHz, so 5 GHz avoids them.

questions.explanation: Interference is signal degradation from other wireless sources or overlapping channels. Non-Wi-Fi sources such as microwaves and cordless phones crowd 2.4 GHz, which is more exposed than 5 GHz.
questions.discriminator_tested: 2.4 GHz is more exposed to non-Wi-Fi interference.

questions.stem: As a user walks to the far end of a building, their laptop's Wi-Fi drops from 5 GHz to 2.4 GHz. What BEST describes the effect on the connection?

options.text: It gains WPA3 protection on the 2.4 GHz band
options.rationale: The band doesn't change the security mode.

options.text: It stays connected because 2.4 GHz penetrates walls better
options.rationale: True, but it leaves out the drop in speed.

options.text: It reaches farther but runs slower on 2.4 GHz
options.rationale: Correct: the range-for-speed trade-off.

options.text: It speeds up because 2.4 GHz is less crowded
options.rationale: 2.4 GHz is slower and usually more crowded.

questions.explanation: 2.4 GHz offers longer range and better penetration but is slower; 5 GHz is faster with shorter range. Dropping to 2.4 GHz keeps the connection at the cost of speed.
questions.discriminator_tested: Range-vs-speed trade-off between bands.

questions.stem: On a WPA2-Enterprise network, which two of these are authentication functions rather than encryption functions? (Choose two.)

options.text: Deriving session keys to scramble the traffic
options.rationale: Session keys serve encryption.

options.text: Checking credentials against RADIUS
options.rationale: Correct: verifies who is connecting.

options.text: Broadcasting the network's SSID
options.rationale: Naming the network is neither.

options.text: Verifying the user's certificate during 802.1X
options.rationale: Correct: proves the user's identity.

options.text: Protecting frames in transit with AES-CCMP
options.rationale: That is encryption: confidentiality of the data.

questions.explanation: Authentication verifies who connects; encryption protects the data. They are separate functions: 802.1X with RADIUS handles identity, while AES-CCMP protects traffic.
questions.discriminator_tested: Authentication = identity; encryption = confidentiality.

questions.stem: A medical cart still uses WEP because its vendor never updated the firmware. Which response is BEST?

options.text: Put it on its own isolated WEP network for now
options.rationale: A reasonable stopgap that limits damage, but the WEP link is still crackable.

options.text: Use WPA with TKIP as a modern replacement
options.rationale: WPA/TKIP is itself an outdated stopgap.

options.text: Use a longer WEP key to make cracking impractical
options.rationale: WEP's flaw is its short IV, not the key length.

options.text: Replace or upgrade it to support WPA2 or WPA3
options.rationale: Correct: WEP has to go; only a modern protocol fixes it.

questions.explanation: WEP is the original wireless security, using RC4 with a short initialization vector. It is broken and obsolete and never acceptable, so the device must move to WPA2 or WPA3.
questions.discriminator_tested: WEP is broken and obsolete; never acceptable.

questions.stem: A legacy access point has the configuration below. Which security generation is it using?
questions.exhibit:
ssid=Legacy
wpa=1
wpa_key_mgmt=WPA-PSK
wpa_pairwise=TKIP
wpa_passphrase=Warehouse2011

options.text: WPA2 with AES-CCMP
options.rationale: WPA2 would show wpa=2 and CCMP.

options.text: WPA3 with SAE
options.rationale: WPA3 would show SAE key management.

options.text: WPA with TKIP
options.rationale: Correct: wpa=1 with TKIP is the original WPA.

options.text: WEP with RC4
options.rationale: WEP doesn't use WPA key management.

questions.explanation: WPA was the interim replacement for WEP, using TKIP so it could run on legacy hardware. It was a stopgap, superseded by WPA2.
questions.discriminator_tested: WPA uses TKIP; superseded by WPA2.

questions.stem: Which change BEST describes what WPA2 introduced over WPA?

options.text: It made Wi-Fi encryption stronger than before
options.rationale: True, but vague; the specific change is AES-CCMP.

options.text: It replaced the PSK handshake with SAE
options.rationale: That is WPA3.

options.text: It added support for the 5 GHz band
options.rationale: Bands come from radio standards, not WPA versions.

options.text: It replaced TKIP and RC4 with AES-CCMP
options.rationale: Correct: AES is the key change.

questions.explanation: WPA2 uses AES-CCMP and is the long-standing standard. AES replaces TKIP and RC4; Personal mode uses a shared passphrase.
questions.discriminator_tested: WPA2: AES replaces TKIP/RC4.

questions.stem: A server logs the entries below each time someone joins the office Wi-Fi. Which Wi-Fi security mode produces entries like these?
questions.exhibit:
radius: Access-Accept  user=asmith@corp  NAS=AP-2F  EAP-PEAP
radius: Access-Reject  user=bjones@corp  NAS=AP-2F  reason=account disabled
radius: Access-Accept  user=cwong@corp   NAS=AP-3E  EAP-TLS

options.text: An open network with a captive portal
options.rationale: A portal login isn't 802.1X EAP authentication.

options.text: WPA2-Personal with a passphrase
options.rationale: A shared passphrase involves no per-user RADIUS checks.

options.text: WPA2-Enterprise using 802.1X
options.rationale: Correct: each user authenticates individually against RADIUS.

options.text: WPA3-Personal using SAE passwords
options.rationale: Personal modes don't use RADIUS.

questions.explanation: WPA2-Enterprise uses 802.1X authentication against a RADIUS server, so each user has individual credentials rather than one shared key; bjones's disabled account is rejected without affecting anyone else.
questions.discriminator_tested: Enterprise = individual credentials per user via RADIUS.

questions.stem: A datasheet says an access point fully implements IEEE 802.11i. Which Wi-Fi Alliance certification BEST corresponds to that?

options.text: WEP
options.rationale: WEP predates 802.11i.

options.text: WPA3
options.rationale: WPA3 goes beyond 802.11i with SAE.

options.text: WPA2
options.rationale: Correct: WPA2 is the certification of 802.11i.

options.text: WPA
options.rationale: WPA implemented only part of an early 802.11i draft.

questions.explanation: 802.11i is the IEEE standard for wireless security that WPA2 implements; WPA2 is the Wi-Fi Alliance certification of it.
questions.discriminator_tested: 802.11i is the standard; WPA2 is its certification.

questions.stem: An attacker captures the handshake of a WPA2-Personal network and runs a cracking tool against it offline. Which change BEST defeats this attack?

options.text: Move to WPA3, whose handshake resists it
options.rationale: Correct: SAE doesn't expose material for offline guessing.

options.text: Use a long, random WPA2 passphrase
options.rationale: Makes cracking much slower, but the handshake can still be attacked offline.

options.text: Switch from TKIP to AES-CCMP
options.rationale: WPA2 already uses AES; the weakness is in the handshake.

options.text: Hide the SSID so the handshake is not broadcast
options.rationale: Hiding the name doesn't hide the handshake.

questions.explanation: WPA3 is the current generation, with a stronger handshake than WPA2. It replaces the PSK handshake and resists offline password guessing.
questions.discriminator_tested: WPA3 resists offline password guessing.

questions.stem: What BEST distinguishes WPA3-Personal from WPA2-Personal?

options.text: It drops the passphrase in favor of certificates
options.rationale: WPA3-Personal still uses a passphrase.

options.text: It uses SAE instead of the PSK handshake
options.rationale: Correct: Simultaneous Authentication of Equals.

options.text: It is the newer and more secure generation
options.rationale: True, but it doesn't name the difference.

options.text: It authenticates each user through RADIUS
options.rationale: That is an Enterprise mode.

questions.explanation: WPA3-Personal is passphrase-based WPA3 using SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) instead of WPA2's PSK handshake.
questions.discriminator_tested: WPA3-Personal uses SAE instead of PSK.

questions.stem: Which two statements describe WPA3-Enterprise? (Choose two.)

options.text: It uses SAE with a shared password
options.rationale: That is WPA3-Personal.

options.text: Everyone on the network shares a single passphrase to join
options.rationale: That describes a Personal mode.

options.text: Each user authenticates through 802.1X and RADIUS
options.rationale: Correct: per-user authentication.

options.text: It is limited to the 2.4 GHz band
options.rationale: Security modes aren't tied to a band.

options.text: It offers an optional 192-bit mode for high security
options.rationale: Correct: the high-security suite.

questions.explanation: WPA3-Enterprise uses 802.1X/RADIUS for per-user authentication with stronger cryptography; its optional 192-bit mode is for high-security use.
questions.discriminator_tested: Enterprise = per-user authentication; 192-bit suite for high security.

questions.stem: Mail from the internet isn't reaching the mail server at 203.0.113.25. The firewall's inbound rules, evaluated top to bottom, are below. What is the MOST likely cause?
questions.exhibit:
1  permit  any -> 203.0.113.20  tcp 443
2  deny    any -> any           any
3  permit  any -> 203.0.113.25  tcp 25

options.text: The firewall is blocking TCP port 25
options.rationale: True as an outcome, but the cause is the rule order.

options.text: The firewall needs a rule permitting UDP 25
options.rationale: SMTP runs over TCP.

options.text: The deny-all rule is evaluated before the mail rule
options.rationale: Correct: rule 2 matches first, so rule 3 is never reached.

options.text: Rule 1 redirects mail traffic to the web server
options.rationale: A permit rule doesn't redirect anything.

questions.explanation: A firewall permits or denies traffic between networks based on rules, evaluated in order. A broad deny placed above a specific permit blocks it; the permit must come first.
questions.discriminator_tested: Firewall = boundary enforcement by rule; order matters.

questions.stem: Which two statements describe a stateless packet-filtering firewall? (Choose two.)

options.text: It automatically allows replies to established sessions
options.rationale: That describes a stateful firewall.

options.text: Return traffic needs its own permit rule
options.rationale: Correct: replies aren't recognized as part of a session.

options.text: It identifies applications regardless of port
options.rationale: That describes a next-generation firewall.

options.text: It records sessions in a state table
options.rationale: A state table is what a stateless firewall lacks.

options.text: It judges each packet on its own
options.rationale: Correct: no memory of earlier packets.

questions.explanation: A stateless (packet-filtering) firewall judges each packet alone on IP, port, and protocol. It has no memory of sessions, so each direction needs a matching rule.
questions.discriminator_tested: Stateless: no memory of sessions.

questions.stem: A reply packet arrives from 198.51.100.10:443 for 10.1.5.22:51544. No inbound rule permits it. Given the firewall's table below, what BEST describes how the firewall handles it?

options.text: Forwards it to the IDS for a decision
options.rationale: An IDS doesn't make forwarding decisions.

options.text: Drops it, because no inbound rule permits it
options.rationale: That is what a stateless filter would do.

options.text: Allows it, because it matches an established session
options.rationale: Correct: the session table entry admits the reply.

options.text: Allows it, because 443 is a common web port
options.rationale: Right action, wrong reason: the port alone admits nothing.

questions.explanation: A stateful firewall tracks connection state and allows return traffic for established sessions. The reply matches the first entry in the state table, so it is allowed without an inbound rule.
questions.discriminator_tested: Stateful remembers sessions and admits return traffic.

questions.stem: A company wants one device to allow web browsing, block file-sharing apps that tunnel over TCP 443, and stop known exploits inside allowed traffic. Which device BEST fits?

options.text: A next-generation firewall
options.rationale: Correct: application awareness plus integrated IPS in one device.

options.text: A stateful firewall on its own
options.rationale: It sees TCP 443, not the application using it.

options.text: A stateful firewall plus a web proxy
options.rationale: Covers some of it with two devices, but neither stops exploits inside allowed traffic.

options.text: A network-based IDS on a SPAN port
options.rationale: It can alert but can't block.

questions.explanation: A next-generation firewall (NGFW) adds application awareness, deep packet inspection, and integrated IPS. It sees applications, not just ports.
questions.discriminator_tested: NGFW sees applications, not just ports.

questions.stem: An infected laptop on the same office switch as a file server starts attacking the server directly. The perimeter firewall never sees this traffic. Which control is BEST placed to block it?

options.text: A host-based firewall on the file server
options.rationale: Correct: it filters traffic arriving at the server itself.

options.text: A stricter rule set on the perimeter firewall
options.rationale: The traffic never crosses the perimeter.

options.text: Moving the server behind an internal network firewall
options.rationale: Would work after a redesign, but nothing in place today can do it.

options.text: An IDS watching the internet link
options.rationale: Wrong place, and an IDS doesn't block.

questions.explanation: A host-based firewall runs on one endpoint and protects that device; a network-based firewall sits at a network boundary and protects a whole segment. Traffic inside one segment never reaches a boundary firewall.
questions.discriminator_tested: Host-based protects one device; network-based protects a segment.

questions.stem: What BEST describes what an IDS does when it detects an attack in progress?

options.text: It logs the event and its details
options.rationale: True, but alerting is the defining action.

options.text: It raises an alert for someone to act on
options.rationale: Correct: detect and alert only.

options.text: It reboots the targeted server
options.rationale: No detection device does that.

options.text: It drops the malicious packets inline
options.rationale: That is an IPS.

questions.explanation: An IDS monitors traffic, typically a passive copy, and alerts on suspicious activity. It detects and alerts only; it does not block.
questions.discriminator_tested: IDS detects and alerts only.

questions.stem: Which two statements are true of an IPS but not of an IDS? (Choose two.)

options.text: It sends alerts about suspicious activity
options.rationale: Both alert.

options.text: It can block malicious traffic itself
options.rationale: Correct: it acts on threats.

options.text: It sits inline in the traffic path
options.rationale: Correct: inline placement.

options.text: It matches traffic against attack signatures
options.rationale: Both can use signatures.

options.text: It inspects a passive copy of the traffic
options.rationale: That describes an IDS.

questions.explanation: An IPS sits inline and blocks detected malicious traffic; an IDS watches a copy and only alerts. Inline placement also means an IPS failure can disrupt traffic.
questions.discriminator_tested: IPS is inline and acts; IDS watches and alerts.

questions.stem: A team is deploying anomaly-based detection on a busy network. Compared with signature-based detection, which drawback should it MOST expect?

options.text: More false positives while baselines are imperfect
options.rationale: Correct: normal-but-unusual activity gets flagged.

options.text: Missing brand-new attacks that have no signature yet
options.rationale: That is the drawback of signature-based detection.

options.text: A learning period before it is effective
options.rationale: Real, but it is the source of the bigger, lasting issue: false positives.

options.text: Needing an inline position to function
options.rationale: Detection method doesn't determine placement.

questions.explanation: Signature-based detection matches known patterns and misses novel attacks; anomaly-based detection flags deviation from a baseline and catches them, but raises more false positives.
questions.discriminator_tested: Anomaly catches novel attacks but raises more false positives.

questions.stem: A school must block adult and gambling sites by category, log which student visited which page, and cache common pages to save bandwidth. Which device BEST fits?

options.text: An anomaly-based IDS on the core switch
options.rationale: Detects unusual activity; doesn't filter or cache.

options.text: A next-generation firewall with URL filtering
options.rationale: Can filter categories and log, but caching is a proxy's job.

options.text: A stateless packet filter at the edge
options.rationale: Sees only addresses and ports.

options.text: A web proxy with content filtering
options.rationale: Correct: it fetches pages for users, filters by category, logs, and caches.

questions.explanation: A proxy server or web filter is an intermediary that makes requests for clients and can filter content. Working at the application level on clients' behalf lets it filter, log per user, and cache.
questions.discriminator_tested: Proxy works at the application level on behalf of clients.
